AboutMe.message1:
I live and work in Paris. My background brings together studies in Computer Systems Engineering and Philosophy, two disciplines that continue to inform my approach to drawing. Neither, however, placed bodily experience at the centre of its inquiry. This is precisely where my artistic project, Gradivas, begins.


Gradivas takes its name from the figure associated with Aby Warburg's understanding of the survival of images: a presence that returns throughout the history of art, carrying traces of desire, emotion and the passions that find expression through the body. This idea of images as vessels of something elemental in human experience — desire, instinct and emotion — persisting beyond their original moment, is central to my practice.


Working primarily with charcoal, sanguine and dry pastel, I approach the body as a place where the invisible takes form. Through gestures, postures and fragments of the human figure, I explore the expressive possibilities that emerge from the relationship between body and soul, between what is revealed and what remains within. Each drawing is part of an ongoing inquiry into the persistence of bodily expression through images.

HowItWorks.message1: A drawing is a knot. A knot is a bond, an in-between, a back-and-forth. For this reason, it cannot be discussed in a homogeneous or univocal manner, since it is instead heterogeneous and equivocal. In other words, the point is not to decipher whether the chicken or the egg came first, but rather to recognize that they are intrinsically bound to one another. In fact, it would not be possible to identify the egg without referring to the other end, the chicken, and vice versa. In a game of tug-of-war, for example, not only would there be no team one without team two, but there would be no game without a rope (figure 1). It is therefore this tension that brings all the elements into play: the rope, team one and team two. Through the force exerted by both ends, it becomes possible to perceive this tension at work; and the stronger it is, the more apparent the situation becomes: two forces directed in opposite directions reveal an inescapable bond (figure 2). In this way, the knot concerns the human condition, since it brings into tension, on the one hand, the mind and, on the other, the flesh. It is from this tension between the two that the body emerges.
HowItWorks.message2:
The knot is a manifestation. For example: «Daniel», who, when asked whether he likes «Lolita», conceals the key to his heart by answering with certainty: «I don't know who you're talking about». Yet his blushing gives him away. Or «Penelope», who, despite having veins bulging on her forehead or while yelling, says that she is not angry. In short, different situations in which the body's disagreement with the mind makes explicit either Daniel's blushing or Penelope's frustration. Thus, the body emerges from the tension between the flesh and the mind, caught in a perpetual tug-of-war between the two. The further one seeks to distance itself from the other, the more expressive the manifestations arising from this tension become. In other words, the flesh-mind tension can only be expressive.


Drawing is nothing more than an extension of the tension between mind and flesh. The more evident the tension, the more forcefully it has been, is, and will be assimilated. Just as the person «Daniel» is a flesh-mind tension, the drawing of «Daniel» also sustains and triggers one or more manifestations. All its elements come to life through the underlying tension, while nevertheless remaining transparent. Every element, every line, every stain (and even the frame itself) is involved in the fabric of the drawing in the same way that the past, the present, the future, relationships and gestures are all constitutive of a body. The surface of the drawing, like the skin, is an in-between: smooth-rough, light-dark, transparent-opaque, white-black, orange-blue.


Drawing is thus tension turned into an image. It is incarnation when it sustains and transmits that same tension to another. It is a knot that later becomes part of the fabric of the one who assimilates it and continues to weave itself.
